\chapter{Review --- Four Small Words, One Instinct}
\label{ch:repaso-juntores}
\hlchaptermodality{235}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can use the small joining words without hesitating.}

I can use the small joining words without hesitating.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[(review)]{(review)}

\label{lesson:ES-C61-repaso-juntores}



\begin{quote}
The two contractions, and nothing else on the list. (\emph{Al}, \emph{del}.)
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four chants. Say each, then say what it does.

\textbf{First.} \emph{Voy al café.} — \emph{A} and \emph{el} fuse, always, and \emph{de} and \emph{el} do the same. Those two, and no third.

\textbf{Second.} \emph{¿Quién es?} — the asking word kept for \textbf{people}, where \emph{qué} would ask about a thing.

\textbf{Third.} \emph{Siete u ocho.} — \emph{O} steps aside as \emph{\textbf{u}} so it is not swallowed by the word after it.

\textbf{Fourth.} \emph{No quiero café ni agua.} — \emph{Ni} carries its own \emph{no}, and two negatives in one Spanish sentence agree rather than cancel.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: one instinct underneath}]
Three of those four are the same instinct wearing different clothes.

\emph{A el} fuses. \emph{De el} fuses. \emph{O} changes shape. In each case a \textbf{small word leaning on a bigger one gives ground}, so that the bigger one stays audible. You saw it first when \emph{mucho} became \emph{muy}.

The fourth is different, and it is the one to keep separate in your head: \emph{ni} is not about sound at all. It is about agreement — once the sentence is negative, its parts stay negative too.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the four chants, in order
  \item \emph{al}, \emph{del}, and then stop — there is no third
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the four is \textbf{not} about sound? (\emph{\textbf{Ni}} — it is about negatives agreeing.)

And what do the other three have in common? (A small word \textbf{gives ground} so the next one stays audible.)
\end{tcolorbox}
